questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: The question an observational study cannot answer
questions.learningObjective: State the limit of observational studies for causation
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: claiming an observational study proves causation; what is the flaw?

options.text: Observational studies cannot rule out confounding
They always have too small a sample

questions.explanation: Without random assignment, confounders remain. Observational studies show association, not causation. Design matters most.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain what randomisation balances
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: thinking random assignment balances only observed covariates; what is wrong?

options.text: It balances only the outcome variable
Randomisation balances both observed and unobserved factors
It balances only sample sizes across groups
It balances nothing without a large sample

questions.explanation: Random assignment balances all factors, measured and unmeasured, in expectation. Sample size affects precision, not the balancing property.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: Define a matched pair
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: confusing matched pairs with independent samples; explain a matched pair.

answer.exemplar: A matched pair links two measurements on the same unit or on closely matched units, so differences remove between-unit variability. Independent samples do not share this link.

questions.explanation: Matching creates dependence that reduces noise. Independent samples lack that link. Choose the design that fits the question.
questions.hint: Same unit measured twice, or matched units.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State the purpose of a placebo
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: in a trial, 60 of 100 placebo recipients improved; what is the placebo response rate as a percentage?
questions.explanation: 60/100 = 60%. The placebo response sets a baseline. Compare treatment to it.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State what blinding prevents
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: omitting blinding in a trial; what bias does blinding reduce?

options.text: Performance and detection bias from knowing assignment
No bias, because blinding is cosmetic

questions.explanation: Blinding keeps participants and assessors unaware of assignment, reducing performance and detection bias. It does not fix selection bias.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: What an interaction in a factorial design means
questions.learningObjective: Define an interaction effect
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: interpreting an interaction as a main effect; what is an interaction?

options.text: The average effect of a single factor
The total sample size in the design
The effect of one factor depends on the level of another

questions.explanation: An interaction means the effect of one factor changes across levels of another. Main effects are averages. Correlation is unrelated.
questions.hint: Effect depends on the other factor's level.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why randomisation beats controls for unmeasured confounders
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: relying only on statistical controls for unmeasured causes; why is randomisation better?

options.text: Controls can adjust for any unmeasured variable
Randomisation balances unmeasured causes in expectation
Unmeasured causes do not affect outcomes

questions.explanation: Controls only adjust for measured factors. Randomisation balances unmeasured ones in expectation. It does not guarantee identical groups.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: The question an observational study cannot answer
questions.learningObjective: Explain why association is not causation
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: inferring causation from an association; explain the gap.

answer.exemplar: Association can arise from confounders, reverse causation, or selection. Causation requires a design or assumption that rules these out, which observation alone rarely provides.

questions.explanation: Confounding and reverse causation mimic association. Design rules them out. Observation alone is weak.
questions.hint: Confounding and reverse causation mimic association.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State the role of random assignment
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: a trial has 200 assigned to treatment and 200 to control; what is the assignment ratio?
questions.explanation: 200/200 = 1. Equal allocation. The ratio is 1. Random assignment supports causal inference.
questions.hint: Divide treatment n by control n.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a matched-pairs design
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: choosing between designs; which is matched pairs?

options.text: A single sample with no comparison
Each subject measured before and after treatment

questions.explanation: Before-after on the same subject is matched pairs. Independent samples and multi-arm trials are different. Match the design to the question.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why placebos are used
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: skipping the placebo arm; why include a placebo?

options.text: To increase the sample size cheaply
To separate treatment effects from expectation effects

questions.explanation: Placebos isolate the treatment effect from placebo responses. They do not inflate significance or bypass ethics. Use them for blinding.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State who should be blinded
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: blinding only participants; who else should be blinded?
questions.explanation: Double-blinding covers participants and assessors; analysis blinding helps too. Participant-only blinding leaves detection bias. Blind broadly.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: What an interaction in a factorial design means
questions.learningObjective: Explain an interaction with an example
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: ignoring interactions; explain what an interaction means.

answer.exemplar: An interaction means the effect of one factor changes depending on another factor's level. For example, a drug may help only when combined with a specific diet, so its benefit is conditional.

questions.explanation: Interactions make effects conditional. Ignoring them can mislead. Test and report them.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State why randomisation handles unmeasured confounders
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: a trial randomises 50 to treatment and 50 to control; what is the total n?
questions.explanation: 50 + 50 = 100. Total sample size. Randomisation supports causal inference at this n.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: The question an observational study cannot answer
questions.learningObjective: State a question only experiments can answer
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: claiming observation answers causal questions; which question needs an experiment?

options.text: What is the correlation between two variables?
What is the prevalence of the outcome?
Does the treatment cause the outcome?
What is the mean of a variable?

questions.explanation: Causal questions need experiments or strong designs. Prevalence, correlation, and means are descriptive or associational. Match method to question.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State a limitation of randomisation in small samples
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: assuming randomisation perfectly balances small samples; what is true?

options.text: Balance applies only to observed variables
Balance is in expectation, not guaranteed in small samples

questions.explanation: Randomisation balances in expectation. Small samples can be imbalanced. It is not useless, just imprecise.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State the analysis for matched pairs
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: analysing matched pairs as independent; what analysis fits?

options.text: A paired t-test on the differences
A one-sample z-test on the mean

questions.explanation: Matched pairs use a paired t-test on differences. Independent tests waste pairing and lose power. Match test to design.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State why a placebo must look identical
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: using a visibly different placebo; explain why identity matters.

answer.exemplar: A placebo must be indistinguishable to maintain blinding. If participants or assessors can tell groups apart, expectation and detection bias return and the trial's validity is compromised.

questions.explanation: Indistinguishability preserves blinding. Visible differences break it. Match appearance, taste, and schedule.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State a bias not fixed by blinding
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: a trial has 10% dropout in treatment and 2% in control; what is the dropout difference in percentage points?
questions.explanation: 10 - 2 = 8 percentage points. Differential dropout threatens validity despite blinding. Track and report attrition.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: What an interaction in a factorial design means
questions.learningObjective: Identify a significant interaction
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: ignoring a significant interaction; what should be done?

options.text: Drop the interaction term to simplify
Ignore it and report only main effects
Interpret effects within levels of the other factor

questions.explanation: With an interaction, main effects are misleading. Interpret simple effects. Do not drop or average over it.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State what randomisation cannot fix
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: thinking randomisation fixes everything; what can it not fix?
questions.explanation: Randomisation balances baseline factors but not post-assignment non-compliance or attrition. Those need other methods. It does balance unmeasured baseline factors.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: The question an observational study cannot answer
questions.learningObjective: State the strength of a randomised experiment
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: preferring observation over experiment for causation; why prefer experiment?
questions.explanation: Experiments use random assignment to break confounding. Size and cost are not the defining advantage. Observation can measure outcomes.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain balance in expectation
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: expecting exact balance from randomisation; explain what actually holds.

answer.exemplar: Randomisation balances covariates in expectation over many hypothetical repetitions, not in any single sample. Imbalance in one trial is expected and does not invalidate the design.

questions.explanation: Balance is an average property. Single-trial imbalance happens. It does not break the design.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: Compute a paired difference
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: a subject scores 72 before and 80 after; what is the paired difference?
questions.explanation: 80 - 72 = 8. Paired differences remove between-subject variability. Analyse these differences.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State the role of a placebo in blinding
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: omitting placebo in a subjective-outcome trial; why is it needed?

options.text: To reduce the sample size needed
To keep participants and assessors blinded

questions.explanation: Placebos enable blinding, which protects subjective outcomes. They do not inflate effects or cut sample size. Use them for validity.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State what double-blinding means
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: using single blinding only; what does double-blinding add?

options.text: Both participants and assessors are unaware of assignment

questions.explanation: Double-blinding keeps both participants and assessors unaware. It is not about analysts or sample size. Blind both sides.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: What an interaction in a factorial design means
questions.learningObjective: State how to detect an interaction
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: looking only at main effects; how is an interaction detected?

options.text: By a significant interaction term in the model

questions.explanation: An interaction term's significance indicates effect modification. R-squared and cell sizes do not detect it. Test the term.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why randomisation supports causal inference
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: doubting randomisation's causal support; explain why it helps.

answer.exemplar: Random assignment makes treatment independent of all baseline factors, measured and unmeasured. That comparability lets differences in outcomes be attributed to treatment rather than confounding.

questions.explanation: Randomisation creates comparability. It supports causal attribution. It does not fix post-assignment issues.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: The question an observational study cannot answer
questions.learningObjective: State a limitation of observational evidence
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: an observational study finds a 20% higher risk; can it claim causation? Flag 1 for yes, 0 for no.
questions.explanation: Observation alone cannot claim causation; flag 0. Confounding may explain the 20%. Need a design or strong assumptions.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State what randomisation balances in expectation
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: thinking randomisation balances only one variable; what does it balance?

options.text: Only variables included in the model
All baseline variables, measured and unmeasured

questions.explanation: Randomisation balances all baseline factors in expectation. Stratification helps precision but is not required for balance.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State when matched pairs are efficient
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: using independent samples when pairs exist; why use matched pairs?

options.text: They always require a smaller sample
They eliminate the need for randomisation
They reduce variability by removing between-unit differences

questions.explanation: Matching removes between-unit variability, improving precision. It does not guarantee normality or remove randomisation needs.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State what a placebo controls for
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: thinking placebo only affects psychology; what does it control for?

options.text: Only the natural history of the disease

questions.explanation: Placebos control for expectation and non-specific effects. They do not fix randomisation or natural history alone. Use them to isolate treatment.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State a bias that persists despite blinding
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: assuming blinding fixes all bias; explain what can persist.

answer.exemplar: Blinding does not fix selection bias, attrition bias, or confounding from non-randomised factors. It targets knowledge of assignment, not the design or retention of participants.

questions.explanation: Blinding is narrow. Selection, attrition, and confounding need other fixes. Design and retention matter too.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: What an interaction in a factorial design means
questions.learningObjective: Compute a simple effect from cell means
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: in a 2x2, cell means are 10 and 14 for factor A at level 1 of B; what is the simple effect?
questions.explanation: 14 - 10 = 4. Simple effect at level 1 of B. Report simple effects when interactions exist.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State why randomisation is preferred over matching for unmeasured factors
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: relying on matching for unmeasured confounders; why prefer randomisation?

options.text: Randomisation balances unmeasured factors; matching cannot
Matching cannot be used in experiments

questions.explanation: Matching only adjusts for measured factors. Randomisation balances unmeasured ones too. Cost and feasibility are separate.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: The question an observational study cannot answer
questions.learningObjective: State a question suitable for observation
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: using experiments for descriptive questions; which question suits observation?

options.text: Is the treatment better than placebo?
What is the prevalence of a condition?

questions.explanation: Prevalence is descriptive and suits observation. Causal questions need experiments. Match method to question.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State the role of stratification
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: skipping stratification; what does stratification improve?

options.text: Balance on key covariates and precision

questions.explanation: Stratification improves balance on key factors and precision. It does not replace randomisation or add subjects. Use it alongside randomisation.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why pairing reduces variance
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: ignoring pairing in analysis; explain why pairing reduces variance.

answer.exemplar: Pairing removes between-unit variability by comparing units to themselves or close matches. The remaining differences are smaller and more precise, improving power for the same sample size.

questions.explanation: Pairing removes between-unit noise. Differences are smaller and more precise. Analyse the pairs.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State why placebo responses occur
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: in a trial, 25 of 100 placebo recipients improved; what is the placebo rate?
questions.explanation: 25/100 = 25%. Placebo responses set the baseline. Compare treatment against it.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State what detection bias is
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: unblinded outcome assessment; what bias arises?

options.text: No bias if assessors are careful

questions.explanation: Unblinded assessment can skew outcome measurement. Blinding prevents it. Carefulness is not enough.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: What an interaction in a factorial design means
questions.learningObjective: State the meaning of no interaction
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: assuming no interaction means no effects; what does no interaction mean?

options.misconception: confuses no interaction with no effects

options.text: Effects are additive and consistent across levels

questions.explanation: No interaction means effects add up consistently. Main effects can still be large. Correlation and cell sizes are separate.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State the role of randomisation in experiments
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: thinking randomisation only balances observed factors; what is its key role?

options.text: It balances unmeasured confounders in expectation
It reduces the need for a control group

questions.explanation: Randomisation's key role is balancing unmeasured confounders. It does not inflate effects or remove controls. Keep a control group.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: The question an observational study cannot answer
questions.learningObjective: Explain confounding in observational studies
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: ignoring confounding; explain why it threatens observation.

answer.exemplar: A confounder affects both exposure and outcome, creating a spurious association. Without randomisation or strong design, observation cannot separate the exposure's effect from the confounder's.

questions.explanation: Confounding mimics or masks effects. Observation alone cannot separate them. Design or strong assumptions are needed.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State what randomisation does not balance
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: a trial randomises 40 to treatment and 60 to control; what is the imbalance in subjects?
questions.explanation: 60 - 40 = 20. Unequal allocation is allowed but changes precision. Randomisation still balances covariates in expectation.
questions.hint: Subtract the smaller from the larger.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State a design that is not matched pairs
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: calling any two groups matched; which is not matched pairs?

options.text: Before and after measurements on one person
Two independent random samples from different populations
Left and right arm of the same person

questions.explanation: Independent samples from different populations are not matched. Before-after, twins, and paired body parts are. Match the design correctly.

questions.learningObjective: State when a placebo is unnecessary
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: using placebo when an active comparator exists; when is placebo unnecessary?

options.misconception: that is when placebo is hardest
objectivity does not remove placebo use

options.text: When an established effective treatment is the ethical comparator

questions.explanation: If an effective treatment exists, ethics may require an active comparator. Objective outcomes reduce but do not eliminate placebo value.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State what performance bias is
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: participants know their assignment; what bias can result?

options.text: No bias if participants are honest

questions.explanation: Knowing assignment can change behaviour, causing performance bias. Blinding prevents it. Honesty is not enough.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: What an interaction in a factorial design means
questions.learningObjective: Explain why interactions matter for policy
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: ignoring interactions in policy; explain why they matter.

answer.exemplar: Interactions mean a treatment's effect varies by context. A policy that works on average may fail or harm some groups, so interactions guide targeted rather than universal recommendations.

questions.explanation: Interactions make effects conditional. Averages can mislead policy. Report and use them.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State why randomisation is not always possible
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: forcing randomisation where unethical; what limits it?

options.text: Randomisation is always possible with enough money
Ethical constraints on assigning harmful exposures
Large samples remove the need for it

questions.explanation: Ethics may prohibit randomising harmful exposures. Money and sample size do not remove constraints. Use observational designs then.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: The question an observational study cannot answer
questions.learningObjective: State the value of observational studies
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: dismissing all observational studies; what are they good for?
questions.explanation: Observational studies generate hypotheses and estimate associations. They do not prove causation. Use them as a first step.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State why balance matters for causal inference
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: ignoring baseline imbalance; why does balance matter?

options.text: It prevents confounding of the treatment effect
It removes the need for a control group

questions.explanation: Balance removes baseline confounding. It does not guarantee significance or normality. Keep a control group.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State a benefit of matched pairs over independent samples
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: choosing independent samples when pairing is possible; explain the benefit of pairs.

answer.exemplar: Matched pairs control for between-unit variability, so treatment effects are detected with greater precision. This often means fewer subjects are needed for the same power.

questions.explanation: Pairing reduces noise and improves power. It can reduce required sample size. Use it when feasible.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State what happens without a placebo
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: a trial without placebo shows 30% improvement; placebo trials show 10%; what is the placebo-adjusted effect?
questions.explanation: 30 - 10 = 20 percentage points. Placebo adjustment isolates the treatment effect. Always include a placebo when possible.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State why double-blinding is preferred
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: using single blinding; why prefer double-blinding?

options.text: It removes the need for a placebo
It blinds both participants and assessors

questions.explanation: Double-blinding covers both sides, reducing more bias. It does not change sample size or remove placebo needs. Blind broadly.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: What an interaction in a factorial design means
questions.learningObjective: State a consequence of ignoring an interaction
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: ignoring an interaction; what can result?

options.text: Misleading average effects that hide subgroup differences

questions.explanation: Ignoring interactions averages over heterogeneous effects, misleading policy. Test and report them. Do not assume no effect.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State how randomisation supports unmeasured confounders
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: thinking only measured confounders matter; why does randomisation help with unmeasured ones?

options.text: It distributes them evenly in expectation across groups
It eliminates them from the population
It makes them irrelevant to outcomes

questions.explanation: Randomisation balances unmeasured confounders in expectation. It does not measure or eliminate them. Distribution is the mechanism.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: The question an observational study cannot answer
questions.learningObjective: Explain the difference between association and causation in observation
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: equating association with causation; explain the difference.

answer.exemplar: Association means variables co-vary; causation means changing one changes the other. Observation shows co-variation but cannot rule out confounders, so causation requires additional design or assumptions.

questions.explanation: Association is co-variation; causation is effect. Observation lacks confounder control. Need design or assumptions.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State the expected outcome of randomisation
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: expecting perfect balance; what does randomisation guarantee?

options.text: Balance in expectation, not in any single sample

questions.explanation: Randomisation balances in expectation over repetitions. Single samples vary. Stratification helps but is not required.

provenance.author: bank-team-statistics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State when matched pairs are inappropriate
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: forcing pairing where units are unrelated; when are matched pairs inappropriate?

options.text: When no natural pairing or matching exists

questions.explanation: Without natural pairing, forced pairing adds noise. Large samples and continuous outcomes do not preclude pairing. Randomisation can coexist.
questions.hint: No natural pairing means no pairs.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.learningObjective: State the ethical consideration of placebo
questions.stem: A researcher fixes a common mistake: using placebo when effective treatment exists; what is the ethical issue?

options.text: Withholding effective treatment may harm participants
Placebos remove the need for consent

questions.explanation: Placebo use is unethical when effective treatment exists and withholding it harms. Placebos are not always unethical. Consent is always required.
